title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Mobile beauty
audience: Mobile beauty therapists who need a base hourly rate and a minimum charge for a treatment visit before they quote.
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill
Calculate a base hourly rate from your own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence
Set a minimum charge for short treatments, and explain it to a client before the visit

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A rate depends on skill, qualifications, the range of treatments offered, the cost of running the business and what clients accept locally. A therapist who brings the treatment to the client’s home saves the client a trip, which can support a higher rate. A narrow range of basic treatments in a crowded area may need a rate closer to local norms. The research found no dated Australian operator price list for mobile beauty. Use your own costs and billable hours first, then compare with local evidence from your own bookings and from the businesses you choose to benchmark against.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between clients, quoting, admin, marketing, training, cleaning equipment, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber gives a general range of about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours as billable (5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). That range is not an Australian figure, so check it against your own log. Illustrative only: 35 paid hours a week over 46 working weeks is 1,610 paid hours. At 60 per cent billable, that is 966 billable hours.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment upkeep, the vehicle, phone, booking software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each will be allowed for, and have a registered tax agent confirm the treatment before you publish a rate. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate. Illustrative only: $60,000 AUD of costs and income needed, divided by 966 billable hours, is $62.11 AUD an hour. AIPT’s personal-training guide (16 May 2025) uses the same working-back method, but its example figures are not used here. Review the base rate about every three months (Business Victoria, undated page).

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short treatments
instruction.body: Short visits can cost more in time than they earn, because travel, set-up and clean-down do not shrink with the length of the treatment. A minimum charge covers the time needed to reach the client and start work. Contractor+ suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, divided by one minus the target margin, so that the minimum covers travel, set-up, clean-down and booking. That source labels its figures illustrative. Illustrative only: a $40 AUD visit cost divided by (1 minus 0.30) gives $57.14 AUD. Round the figure on your price sheet, state it before the visit and explain it in plain words.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, booking software and marketing.
Add the income you need, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short treatment, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only. A mobile beauty therapist has 1,610 paid hours a year but can bill only 60 of every 100 paid hours. The therapist sets the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Using all 1,610 paid hours gives $60,000 AUD divided by 1,610, which is $37.27 AUD an hour. That figure looks reasonable but cannot be earned, because only 966 hours are billable. The costs and income must come out of billable work, which gives $62.11 AUD an hour. The wrong assumption understates the rate by about two-fifths. Check the rate against the minimum charge and the local evidence before it is published.

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a marketplace listing or a competitor’s price without checking your own costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short treatments at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Misleading price statements are prohibited (ACCC, Setting prices: what’s allowed, 15 July 2026). The sources read do not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before you publish a price sheet.
Confirm the treatment of leave, superannuation and tax with a registered tax agent. This is not confirmed by any source read for this lesson.

This lesson does not grant any licence. Pricing a treatment you are not qualified or registered to deliver in your state is outside this lesson, and the registration rules are set by each state and territory.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from your costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short treatment.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short treatments.

knowledgeChecks.question: A therapist can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per treatment
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short treatments?
options: Because short treatments need travel but no set-up time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the length of the treatment
Because clients expect every treatment to cost the same amount, whatever its length
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every treatment the therapist takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: Team 4 hourly-rate research (/home/claude/tasks/team4-R-hourly-rate-tactics.md) and personal-services research for beauty (/home/claude/tasks/team4-V-personal-services-a.md), both 2026-11-09. Only sources read in those files are listed.

business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure.

Jobber Academy, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. Supports: a general range of 60 to 80 per cent billable; not an Australian figure.

AIPT, 'Personal Training Prices: Setting the Right Rates', https://www.aipt.edu.au/articles/personal-training-prices-how-much-should-you-charge, 16 May 2025. Supports: work backwards from a target income, with tax and business costs added on top. Example figures not used.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor’s Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Supports: minimum from full visit cost divided by one minus target margin; the source labels its figures illustrative.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what’s allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements prohibited.

Gaps: no dated Australian operator rate or minimum charge for mobile beauty; ACCC guidance on minimum or call-out charges not found; tax treatment of leave and superannuation not confirmed. Illustrative figures ($60,000, 60 per cent billable, 46 weeks, 35 hours, $40 visit cost) are assumptions for teaching only.
